Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: Jay, a 22-year-old South Eastern Asian male and UX Designer, has been grappling with the aftermath of a natural disaster that occurred several months ago. On the day of the traumatic event, he was at work when the ground began to shake violently, causing chaos in his office building. He recalls feeling an intense sense of vulnerability as debris fell around him, and he could taste dust in the air—a sensation that has haunted him ever since. Since the disaster, Jay experiences a recurring trigger whenever he feels neck pain or physical discomfort. These sensations often bring back vivid memories of the event, making it feel almost surreal as if it didn’t actually happen to him. He can still taste the dust and dirt from that day, which adds to his disorientation. This connection between his somatic symptoms and traumatic memories has led Jay to distrust others and believe they are not what they seem, further isolating himself. Jay’s isolation is a direct result of these triggers and memories, as he finds it increasingly difficult to engage with colleagues at work without feeling overwhelmed by the past event. The taste of dust and the neck pain often coincide, leading him to feel emotionally intense reactions without any clear visual memory, which deepens his sense of disconnection from others and places. His distrust extends beyond just colleagues; Jay has started avoiding social gatherings altogether. He feels set apart from others, as if he no longer belongs anywhere. This isolation is reinforced by the recurrent triggers, leading him to avoid situations that might elicit physical discomfort or pain. His fear of reliving the traumatic event through these triggers makes it nearly impossible for him to maintain meaningful connections with friends and family. Jay’s occupation as a UX Designer has been particularly affected. He finds himself struggling to focus on work tasks when his neck pain flares up, often leading to moments where he feels the full emotional intensity of the disaster without any visual cues. This has resulted in several missed deadlines and projects that were handed off due to his inability to concentrate. The memory quality—feeling as if it didn’t actually happen to him—has further compounded his sense of isolation and distrust. He is certain that people around him do not understand what he went through, leading him to believe they cannot be trusted with his thoughts or feelings. This belief makes it difficult for Jay to seek help or confide in others about his struggles. Jay’s current state has reached a critical point where the cumulative effects of isolation and distrust have made daily life unbearable. He is most afraid that he will never truly escape the trauma, always feeling like an outsider. At the same time, he hopes for a way to regain trust and connection with others without reliving the painful memories every day. It was this deepening sense of disconnection and fear that finally brought Jay to seek help, recognizing that his daily life is increasingly being consumed by the lingering effects of the disaster. He yearns to reclaim a sense of belonging and normalcy in his relationships and work, but fears the cycle will continue unless he finds a way to break it.
